about: Side topic X1 (What engineering lies beneath the system?): eight components, the discipline that designs each, two questions it answers and what system models borrow from it. Numbers are read from the lessons that teach them (F4, F5, A16, lesson 13 and Prairie Town); this file holds words and reading only. Physics, operations and uses only: no cost, timing or deployment of any technology.

kinds.label: Rating
kinds.text: How much it can make, carry or store: MW, MWh, a line's limit.

kinds.label: Efficiency
kinds.text: How much of what goes in comes out: a heat rate, a round trip, kWh per kilogram.

kinds.label: Ramp limit
kinds.text: How fast its output can change, in MW per hour.

kinds.label: Minimum load
kinds.text: The lowest output it can hold steadily, as a share of its size; below that it must stop.

kinds.label: Outlet temperature
kinds.text: How hot the heat it gives is, which sets the uses that heat can serve.

kinds.label: Reliability and life
kinds.text: Three separate numbers: how often it fails, how long each outage lasts, and how many years it serves before replacement.

kinds.label: Operating rule
kinds.text: How the people and software running the grid decide: time steps, reserves, limits.

components.label: Inverter
qs: How does it turn the direct current of solar panels and batteries into alternating current?
How fast can it respond, and does it hold on through a voltage dip?
components.text: Its AC rating, its conversion losses, how fast it can change output and, in A17, whether it forms or follows the grid.
components.read: Erickson and Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics (Springer)

components.label: Protective relay
qs: Which [[circuit-breaker|breaker]] should open, and how fast, when a line has a [[fault|fault]]?
How are its settings chosen so that healthy lines stay in service?
components.text: Not the relay settings: equipment ratings, such as a line's thermal rating, and how often equipment is forced out of service.
components.read: Horowitz and Phadke, Power System Relaying (Wiley)

components.label: Turbine blade
qs: How much of the wind's power can the rotor catch?
Will the blade survive repeated gusts over its intended life?
components.text: A power curve with its rated power, and how often the turbines are available.
components.read: Burton, Jenkins, Sharpe and Bossanyi, Wind Energy Handbook (Wiley)

components.label: Gas-turbine combustor
qs: How hot can the flame burn before metal or emission limits are reached?
How low can the turbine run and still burn steadily?
components.text: A heat rate, a ramp limit, a minimum load and a start time.

components.label: Reactor core
components.discipline: Reactor physics, thermal hydraulics and nuclear materials
qs: How does the core hold its chain reaction steady?
How is heat carried away so that the fuel and the metal tubes that hold it stay within their limits?
components.text: A thermal and an electric rating, an outlet temperature and a heat rate.
components.read: Lamarsh and Baratta, Introduction to Nuclear Engineering (Pearson)

components.label: Electrolyzer stack
qs: How much electricity does a kilogram of hydrogen take?
How fast do the cells wear, and how low can the stack run?
components.text: Electricity per kilogram of hydrogen for the whole system (stack, power supply, pumps and dryers), a minimum load and a stack life.
components.read: U.S. Department of Energy, Hydrogen and Fuel Cell Technologies Office, Hydrogen Production: Electrolysis (energy.gov)

components.label: Battery cell
qs: How much energy does a cell hold, and how fast can it charge?
How do heat and cycling age it?
components.text: A round-trip efficiency for the whole battery system, a duration (energy over power) and a life.

components.label: Control room
qs: How do operators see the grid every few seconds and send each plant its target output?
How are those systems kept safe from cyberattack?
components.text: Operating rules: how often dispatch runs, how much reserve is held and which limits are watched.
components.read: Wood, Wollenberg and Sheblé, Power Generation, Operation, and Control (Wiley)

predict.q: What does a planner take from the blade engineers

options.label: The layers of glass and carbon fiber in each blade
The farm's power curve and how often it is available

feedback.a: No: the layup is the structural engineers' design; a model needs the output it leads to.
feedback.b: Yes: models borrow numbers such as a power curve, its rated power and availability, not the design.
feedback.c: No: the tests show the blade will last; a model takes the result as availability and a life.

cards.why: Borrowed: fuel per MWh is how a dispatch model prices the plant's output.

cards.text: The shape of the combustor's flame
cards.why: Kept: combustion engineers shape it; the model sees only the heat rate and emissions it leads to.
Borrowed: it sets how much of each MWh sent into storage comes back out.

cards.text: The coating on a battery's electrodes
cards.why: Kept: a materials choice; the model sees its effect on efficiency and life.
Borrowed: wind speed in, MW out, hour by hour.

cards.text: The fiber layup inside a blade
cards.why: Kept: a structural design; the model sees availability and life.

cards.text: An electrolyzer's kWh per kilogram of hydrogen
cards.why: Borrowed: it turns MWh of electricity into kilograms of hydrogen.

cards.text: The catalyst inside an electrolyzer cell
cards.why: Kept: electrochemists choose it; the model sees its kWh per kilogram and stack life.

cyber.q: Do NERC's mandatory cybersecurity standards cover a home's rooftop solar inverter on a local feeder

options.label: Yes, every inverter on the grid
Generally not: they cover the bulk power system's cyber systems
Only when the home sells power

feedback.a: No: NERC's Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) standards apply only to bulk electric system cyber systems, and in general not to systems on the distribution grid.
feedback.b: Right: NERC's Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) standards apply only to bulk electric system cyber systems, and in general not to systems on the distribution grid.
feedback.c: No: selling power does not change it; NERC's Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) standards apply to bulk electric system cyber systems, in general not to distribution.
